name: Hawaiian religion
info: Hawaiian religion, also known as the kapu system, comprises the Indigenous beliefs and practices of Native Hawaiians: a polytheistic tradition with Kāne, Kū, Lono and Kanaloa among its chief gods, brought by Polynesian settlers between 500 and 1300 CE.

facts.origin: The Hawaiian Islands, brought by Tahitians and other Pacific Islanders who landed there between 500 and 1300 CE; there is significant evidence of settlement no later than 800 CE, with immigration continuing to about 1300 CE, from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia.
facts.founder: none: it arose among Polynesian settlers and evolved over time and from place to place; tradition says the kapu system arrived with Pāʻao, a priest or chief from Tahiti, around 1200 CE.
facts.scriptures: none written: the Kumulipo, an epic chant linking the aliʻi, or Hawaiian royalty, to the gods, and the prayers, chants and traditions of the kahuna and families, handed down orally.
facts.followers: No figure is given: traditional practices survive through family ʻaumākua, the veneration of iwi (bones) and the care of sacred places; some Hawaiians practise Christianised versions of old traditions, others the old faith as a co-religion.

t: Hawaiian religion is polytheistic and animistic: Kāne, Kū, Lono and Kanaloa are especially prominent among many gods, and every Native Hawaiian family was considered to have one or more guardian spirits, the ʻaumākua.

The kapu system, a set of taboos separating the spiritually pure from the potentially unclean, ruled daily life until 1819, when Kamehameha II, persuaded by two of his father's wives and the kahuna nui Hewahewa, overthrew it.

Missionaries arrived from 1820 and most aliʻi converted, but family ʻaumākua, veneration of bones and sacred places survived, and a Hawaiian Renaissance in the 1970s brought a resurgence of the religion.
dyk: In the Kumulipo, the man Kiʻi succeeds in seducing and reproducing with the woman Laʻilaʻi before the god Kāne has the chance, so the divine lineage becomes younger than, and subservient to, the lineage of humankind.
ev: Settlers from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia have reached the Hawaiian Islands by this date, bringing their religious beliefs
By tradition Pāʻao, a priest or chief from Tahiti, arrives in Hawaiʻi and brings the kapu system
After the death of Kamehameha the Great, Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani confer with the kahuna nui Hewahewa and persuade Liholiho, Kamehameha II, to overthrow the kapu system
Protestant Christian missionaries begin to arrive from the United States and gain great influence in the Kingdom of Hawaii
The American author Max Freedom Long originates the philosophy and practice he calls Huna
Members of Protect Kahoʻolawe ʻOhana file suit over the Navy's use of Kahoʻolawe for target practice, citing cultural and religious sites
The unearthing of 1,000 graves during construction of a hotel on Maui leads to its redesign and relocation inland
Protests begin on the Island of Hawaii over the choice of Mauna Kea for the Thirty Meter Telescope

sections.origins:
Hawaiian religion comprises the Indigenous religious beliefs and practices of Native Hawaiians, and is also known as the kapu system. It was based partly on the tapu system common in Polynesia and likely originated among the Tahitians and other Pacific Islanders who landed in Hawaiʻi between 500 and 1300 CE. It is unclear when settlers first came, but there is significant evidence that the islands were settled no later than 800 CE and that immigration continued to about 1300 CE. Settlers came from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia, and at some point a significant influx of Tahitians brought their religious beliefs with them.

Early Hawaiian religion resembled other Polynesian religions in being largely focused on natural forces such as the tides, the sky and volcanic activity, and on human dependence on nature for subsistence. The major early gods reflected this: early Hawaiians worshipped Kāne, god of the sky and creation, Kū, god of war and male pursuits, Lono, god of peace, rain and fertility, and Kanaloa, god of the ocean.

The people were spread among eight islands, with waves of immigration over hundreds of years, so religious practices evolved over time and from place to place. The scholar Mary Kawena Pukui, raised in Kaʻū, maintained that the early Hawaiian gods were benign.
sections.beliefs:
Hawaiian religion is polytheistic, with a belief in many deities and spirits, including the animistic belief that spirits are found in non-human animals and natural elements such as the waves and the sky. Kāne, Kū, Lono and Kanaloa are especially prominent; other notable deities include Laka, Kihawahine, Haumea, Papahānaumoku and, most famously, Pele. Every Native Hawaiian family was considered to have one or more guardian spirits, the ʻaumākua. The historian June Gutmanis sorted the pantheon into six groups, from the four gods (ka hā) to the guardians, while Jay Kauka described three: the four gods, many lesser gods (kupua) tied to professions, and the ʻaumakua of families. Not all ancient Hawaiians believed in deities: some were atheists, called ʻaia.

Prayer was an essential part of life, said when building a house, making a canoe or giving lomilomi massage. Lono was worshipped during the Makahiki season and Kū in times of war. The usual posture, sitting upright with head high and eyes open, has been read as a relationship of respect and self-respect, with the ʻaumākua bridging the gap between gods and people.

Heiau were the focal points for prayer. Offerings, sacrifices and prayers were made at these temples, at thousands of koʻa (shrines), at many wahi pana (sacred places) and at small kuahu (altars) in homes.
sections.texts:
Hawaiian tradition is oral. One creation myth is embodied in the Kumulipo, an epic chant that links the aliʻi, or Hawaiian royalty, to the gods. It is divided into two sections: night, or pō, which corresponds to divinity, and day, or ao, which corresponds to humankind. After the birth of Laʻilaʻi, the woman, and Kiʻi, the man, the man succeeds in seducing and reproducing with the woman before the god Kāne has a chance, making the divine lineage younger than, and subservient to, the lineage of humankind. This is read as the passage of humankind from being symbols for the gods (the literal meaning of kiʻi) into keepers of those symbols in the form of idols and the like. The Kumulipo was recited at the time of Makahiki, to honour Lono, the god of fertility.

Other voices come through prayer and spirit-speech. Histories of the 19th century describe prayer throughout the day, with set prayers for sleeping, eating, drinking and travelling. In 1867 the kahuna Kūpaʻiulu of Maui described a counter-sorcery ritual to heal someone made ill by hoʻopiʻopiʻo, another person's evil thoughts: a kapa cloth was shaken and prayers were said, and if the evil spirit appeared and possessed the patient, the practitioner could save them by speaking with it.

Writers on the tradition include Pukui, and Pali Jae Lee, who describes the ancient time as one of family and oneness with all things.
sections.spread:
Hawaiian religion came to the islands with settlers from the Marquesas and greater Polynesia and with a significant influx of Tahitians, in the centuries to about 1300 CE. Tradition holds that the kapu system arrived with Pāʻao, a priest or chief from Tahiti who came around 1200 CE.

The kapu system stayed in place until 1819. After the death of Kamehameha the Great that year, two of his wives, Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani, then the most powerful people in the kingdom, conferred with the kahuna nui Hewahewa. They persuaded the young Liholiho, Kamehameha II, to overthrow it, and the people were ordered to burn the wooden statues and tear down the rock temples. Without the hierarchical system in place, some abandoned the old gods, while others kept worshipping them, especially their family ʻaumākua.

Protestant Christian missionaries arrived from the United States from 1820 and eventually gained great political, moral and economic influence in the Kingdom of Hawaii. Most of the aliʻi, among them Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani, converted. It took 11 years for Kaʻahumanu to proclaim laws against ancient religious practices, forbidding the worship of idols and ancient gods, the hula, chant and song, and the planting and drinking of ʻawa.

In the 1970s the religion experienced a resurgence during the Hawaiian Renaissance.
sections.community:
The kahuna were respected, educated individuals who formed a class in the social hierarchy, serving the King and the courtiers and assisting the makaʻāinana, the common people. Kahuna were often healers, navigators, builders, prophets or temple workers and philosophers, and they also talked with the spirits. Pukui and others believed that kahuna did not have the mystical transcendent experiences described in other religions: possession was a trance-like state but a communion with known spirits.

Kapu was a system of taboos designed to separate the spiritually pure (laʻa) from the potentially unclean (haumia). It imposed restrictions on daily life: the separation of men and women at mealtimes (ʻaikapu), restrictions on gathering and preparing food, the separation of menstruating women, restrictions on looking at, touching or being close to chiefs and people of known spiritual power, and limits on overfishing. Women were forbidden to eat pig, coconut, banana and certain red foods because of their male symbolism.

Punishments for breaking the kapu could include death, though a person who escaped to a puʻuhonua, a city of refuge, could be saved. The kahuna nui mandated long periods of absolute silence in the village, when no baby could cry, dog howl or rooster crow on pain of death. In wartime the first two men killed were offered to the gods, and human sacrifice was not unknown.
sections.legacy:
After the kapu fell and the missionaries came, a number of traditions survived through integration, practice in hiding or practice in rural communities. They include the worship of family ancestral gods, the ʻaumākua, the veneration of iwi (bones) and the preservation of wahi pana, sacred places. Hula, at one time outlawed as a religious practice, is today performed in both spiritual and secular contexts. Some Hawaiians practise Christianised versions of old traditions, and others practise the old faith as a co-religion. Today Hawaiian religious practices are protected by the American Indian Religious Freedom Act.

In the 1930s the American author Max Freedom Long originated a philosophy and practice he called Huna. Long and his successors represent it as a type of ancient Hawaiian occultism, but the scholars Rothstein and Chai consider it a New Age mix of cultural appropriation and fantasy, not representative of traditional Hawaiian religion.

Traditional beliefs have played a role in the politics of Hawaiʻi since contact. In 1976 the suit Aluli et al. v. Brown forced the Navy to survey and protect important sites on Kahoʻolawe and allow limited access for religious purposes. After 1,000 graves, dating back to 850 CE, were unearthed on Maui in 1988, a hotel was moved inland. Since 2014 protests have continued over Mauna Kea, which some Hawaiians regard as the most sacred mountain of their religion; practitioners have repeatedly failed in court to prove that these practices predate 1893.

summary: Hawaiian religion, also called the kapu system, is the polytheistic, animistic faith of Native Hawaiians, with Kāne, Kū, Lono and Kanaloa among its chief gods and family guardian spirits called ʻaumākua. The kapu system was overthrown in 1819; traditions survived through families and sacred places and revived from the 1970s.
references: Martha Warren Beckwith, The Kumulipo: A Hawaiian Creation Chant (University of Hawaii Press, 1981)
David Malo, Hawaiian Antiquities (Bishop Museum Press, 2005)
Patrick Vinton Kirch, A shark going inland is my chief: the island civilization of ancient Hawaiʻi (University of California Press, 2012)
notes: Start: the lede says Tahitians and other Pacific Islanders landed between 500 and 1300 CE, the Origins section says settlement no later than 800 CE with immigration to about 1300 CE, and the kapu is tied to Pāʻao around 1200. I used 800, circa, with the event 'c. 800'. These are not reconciled in the article.
The article spells the ʻaumākua both ʻaumākua and ʻaumakua; Pāʻao and Liholiho as given. Gutmanis's six groups are summarised, not listed in full.
The article gives no number of followers; the facts line says so by describing what survives.
The Atheism section ('ʻaia') and the sentence that kahuna were 'respected' are kept as the article has them. Pukui's view that early gods were benign is attributed, not stated as fact.
The 1820 missionary arrival and the 'it took 11 years' for Kaʻahumanu's laws are as stated; the article gives no calendar year for the laws, so none is given.
The article's 'Huna' text says 'protected by the American Indian Religious Freedom Act'; no date given. The Mauna Kea paragraph gives the courts' finding about the 1893 threshold as the article does.

Faith map: the Marquesas and Tahiti routes use general coordinates; their years (800, 1200) follow the article's hedged settlement dates. Only the 1819 end of the kapu, as the article dates it, changes the islands' level from 2 to 1.
Left out: the article's quoted passages by Lee and on 'Supreme Being'; the detail of the ʻAikapu myth of Wākea, Papa and Hoʻohokukalani and the first taro; Niʻaupiʻo.
